headline: Trulieve, Curaleaf and 3 more MSOs carry $1.96B in disputed 280E tax
dek: Third-quarter filings from five big US cannabis operators show $1.96B in uncertain tax balances and three different start dates for rescheduling relief.
key_points: Trulieve, Curaleaf, Verano, Ascend Wellness and Vireo Growth reported about $1.96 billion in uncertain tax balances at 30 September, a Marijuana Herald review of their filings found.
Treasury and the IRS said on 23 April that guidance would give full-year relief for 2026, but that guidance has still not been issued.
The companies disagree on when relief starts: Trulieve books all of 2026, Vireo from 23 April and Curaleaf from 28 April.
No federal decision has been made on relief for years before 2026, which is where most of the $1.96 billion sits.
body: Five of the largest US cannabis operators are carrying close to $2 billion in tax positions that the IRS has never accepted, more than six months after medical marijuana moved to Schedule III. Trulieve, Curaleaf, Verano, Ascend Wellness and Vireo Growth reported a combined $1.96 billion in uncertain tax balances at 30 September in quarterly filings released over the past three weeks, according to an analysis The Marijuana Herald published on 14 November.

The same filings show the companies reading federal policy in three different ways. Trulieve is booking rescheduling tax relief for all of 2026, Curaleaf only from 28 April, and Vireo from 23 April. The reason is simple: the Treasury Department and the IRS promised formal guidance in April, and it has not arrived.
## Where the $1.96 billion sits

Trulieve carries the largest balance. It reported $625.4 million in net uncertain tax liabilities at the end of September, of which about $610 million relates to its challenge to Section 280E, the tax rule that bars businesses trafficking in Schedule I or II drugs from deducting ordinary expenses. The total includes $104.8 million in accrued interest. Trulieve is also contesting about $38.1 million in proposed IRS penalties against some subsidiaries, which are not in that figure, the Herald reported.

Curaleaf reported $476.1 million, including interest and penalties, down $55.4 million since the end of 2025. Verano reported $410.9 million, up from $378.3 million at year-end. Ascend reported $231.4 million in unrecognised tax benefits, up from $203.9 million, plus a separate $53.6 million in accrued interest and penalties. Vireo reported $215.8 million, up from $120 million at the end of 2025.

By MetaFlora's calculation, Trulieve alone accounts for about 32% of the five-company total. Vireo's balance rose about 80% in nine months, the fastest increase in the group. Verano's rose about 9% and Ascend's about 13%. Curaleaf is the only one of the five whose balance fell.

These are accounting reserves, not tax bills. The companies have taken the position on their returns that they may deduct normal business costs, and accounting rules require them to record a liability for the chance the IRS disagrees. The figures are also not calculated the same way: some include interest and penalties and some do not.
> The rescheduling order fixed 2026. It did nothing yet for the years when these balances were built.
## Three readings of one press release

On 23 April the Treasury and the IRS said they plan to issue guidance on the tax effects of the Justice Department's final order, which moved state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III effective 28 April. The agencies said the guidance is expected to include a transition rule treating rescheduling as applying for a business's full taxable year that includes the order's effective date. For a calendar-year company, that means 1 January 2026.

Trulieve, which since June reports only its medical operations, has taken the agencies at their word. It says recent federal developments give enough support under accounting standards to recognise relief for all of 2026. It has not reduced its reserves for earlier years.

Curaleaf has gone the other way. Its management concluded the April announcement is not authoritative guidance, so it recognises relief for qualifying medical activity only from 28 April. It keeps reserves for medical activity earlier in the year, for adult-use activity and for prior years. Curaleaf also disclosed that the IRS is examining some of its returns for 2020 to 2024, and warned that the final bill could substantially exceed its reserves if its 280E position fails, according to the Herald.

Vireo has picked a third date, 23 April, when the order was signed rather than when it took effect. It said about $55 million of its balance built up on medical activity between 29 August 2023, when health officials recommended Schedule III, and 22 April 2026. Verano and Ascend said they are still evaluating the effect of rescheduling on past positions.
## Why the old years matter most

The bulk of the $1.96 billion relates to years before 2026, and federal policy has not touched them. The Justice Department's April order encouraged Treasury to consider retroactive 280E relief for state medical licensees. Treasury's own statement said only that it would issue guidance and did not commit to retroactive relief.

For investors, that leaves a wide range of outcomes. If Treasury grants some retroactive relief for medical activity, parts of these reserves could be released into earnings. If it does not, and the IRS presses its audits, companies could face cash demands far larger than their current tax payments. Trulieve, for comparison, ended the third quarter with $327 million in cash, about half its reported uncertain tax liability, according to its 5 November results release.

The issue is wider than five companies. In October, a Marijuana Herald review of 15 listed operators counted $2.82 billion in uncertain tax liabilities at 30 June, with 12 of the 15 reporting increases in the first half of the year. We covered Vireo's and Ascend's third-quarter results on 10 and 13 November; their tax notes show the same pattern of current-year relief alongside growing legacy balances.
## Adult-use is still stuck

Adult-use sales remain in Schedule I and fully subject to 280E. That matters most for operators with large recreational businesses, which must also wait for the promised rules on how to split expenses between medical and adult-use activity. A separate DEA proceeding on moving all marijuana to Schedule III finished its evidentiary hearing in July, and supplemental briefing closed this month. The administrative law judge's recommended decision is the next step.
## What to watch

The Treasury-IRS guidance is the single biggest item: its timing, whether it confirms full-year 2026 relief, how it handles mixed medical and adult-use operators, and whether it says anything about earlier years. Watch for the DEA judge's recommendation on broader rescheduling, which would decide whether adult-use activity escapes 280E. And watch year-end filings in February and March: if Curaleaf and Vireo move to Trulieve's full-year approach, it will signal that auditors now see the April statement as enough.
